rows: Requests recorded as incidents corrupt every incident metric: MTTR, reopen rate, priority distribution and Problem clustering all include work that was never a failure. Usually indicates the catalogue is too hard to use. *Detect:* Incidents whose category, close code or description pattern indicates a request rather than a disruption. *Confidence:* 85% — classification from category and text pattern; report with samples. *Guard:* Categories genuinely ambiguous between request and incident. *Lane 2 for catalogue and form configuration, Lane 3 for behaviour.*
Catalogue items with no fulfilment workflow

The request is submitted and nothing happens. It sits in a queue until someone notices, and the requester assumes the system is broken. *Detect:* Active catalogue items with no workflow, flow or fulfilment task generation. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Fulfilment by manual assignment as a deliberate model. *Lane 2.*
Request fulfilment with no target or SLA

Requests have no measured turnaround, so the request practice cannot be reported on at all. *Detect:* Request items with no SLA definition covering them. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Deliberately unmeasured low-priority items. *Lane 2.*
Request approval routed to inactive users or empty groups

Requests hang indefinitely. Requesters learn to route around the catalogue, which produces ITIL-001 and shadow fulfilment. *Detect:* Approval configuration resolving to inactive users or zero-member groups. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Grace period with a delegate. *Lane 3.* Joins DQ-095, DQ-096.

Requests age more quietly than incidents because nobody is escalating. Ageing backlog here is a satisfaction problem before it is an operational one. *Detect:* Open request items beyond age threshold by type. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Items awaiting a scheduled fulfilment window. *Lane 3.*
Fulfilment tasks created and never completed

The parent request shows in progress while its tasks are stalled. The requester sees activity and nothing arrives. *Detect:* Open fulfilment tasks beyond age threshold with their parent request state. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Sequenced tasks with future start dates. *Lane 3.*
Requests closed with no fulfilment evidence

No record of what was actually delivered. Disputes about whether a request was fulfilled cannot be resolved. *Detect:* Closed requests with empty close notes and no completed fulfilment task. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Automated fulfilment with evidence in the workflow context. *Lane 2.*
Standard request types handled as ad-hoc

Repeatable requests handled without a catalogue item. Each one is fulfilled differently, at full cost, with no reusable path. *Detect:* Request or incident clusters by description similarity with no corresponding catalogue item. *Confidence:* 85% — clustering confidence. *Guard:* Genuinely one-off requests that happen to be similarly worded. *Lane 3.*

Nobody maintains the item. When fulfilment breaks, or the underlying service changes, nothing updates. *Detect:* Active items with empty owner. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Ownership at category level. *Lane 3.* Joins DQ-091.
Request reopen or rework rate above threshold

The request was fulfilled and the requester came back. Either the item specification is unclear or fulfilment is inconsistent. *Detect:* Reopened or duplicate follow-up requests as a share of fulfilled volume, by item. *Confidence:* 100% on the ratio; duplicate-follow-up detection at 85%. *Guard:* Legitimate sequential requests. *Lane 3.*
Variables collected but never used by fulfilment

The requester fills in fields nobody reads. Adds friction to the request and captures nothing. *Detect:* Catalogue variables with no reference in the fulfilment workflow or task content. *Confidence:* 90%. *Guard:* Variables read by a fulfiller manually. *Lane 3.*
Fulfilment groups with zero active members

The same failure as ITSM-018 in the request channel, where it is less visible because requests escalate less readily. *Detect:* Fulfilment groups resolving to zero active members. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Group in transition. *Lane 3.*

Catalogue clutter that suppresses use of the items that matter. *Detect:* Active items with zero orders beyond 365 days. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Seasonal or emergency items. *Lane 3.* Joins DQ-123.
No self-service fulfilment for high-volume repeatable requests

The highest-volume requests consume fulfiller time on work that could be automated. The measurable version of "the service desk is overloaded". *Detect:* Top request types by volume with fully manual fulfilment. *Confidence:* 100% on volume; automation feasibility is advisory. *Guard:* Items requiring human judgement. *Lane 3.*

The fulfilment task carries none of the request detail, so the fulfiller opens the parent or asks again. *Detect:* Fulfilment tasks with no variable content or description inherited from the request. *Confidence:* 90%. *Guard:* Fulfillers working from the parent by design. *Lane 2.*
No distinction between request and service request in the data model

Everything is one undifferentiated pool, so request reporting cannot separate access requests from hardware from information. *Detect:* Request type or category distribution showing no meaningful differentiation. *Confidence:* 100% on the distribution. *Guard:* Small catalogue where differentiation adds nothing. *Lane 2.*
Catalogue not aligned to the CSDM service model

The catalogue offers things the service model does not contain, and the service model contains services the catalogue does not offer. Two views of the same portfolio that cannot be reconciled. *Detect:* Set comparison between catalogue categories/items and CSDM service and offering records. *Confidence:* 90% — matching relies on naming. *Guard:* Catalogue deliberately a consumer-facing subset. *Lane 3.* Joins CSDM-016.
Items not mapped to a service or offering

The request cannot be attributed to a service, so demand, cost and impact per service all exclude request volume. *Detect:* Catalogue items with no service or offering reference. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Internal administrative items. *Lane 1 where inferable, Lane 3 otherwise.*
Business and technical catalogue not separated

Consumers see technical items they cannot act on, and technical fulfilment paths are exposed to the wrong audience. *Detect:* Catalogue structure with no audience or user-criteria differentiation across technical and business items. *Confidence:* 90%. *Guard:* Deliberate single catalogue for a technical audience. *Lane 2.*
Items with no review date or expired review

The item describes a service as it was. Pricing, fulfilment path and eligibility all drift. *Detect:* Active items with no review date or a review date in the past. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* External review process. *Lane 3.*
User criteria absent, so all items are visible to everyone

Requesters see items they are not entitled to, submit them, and the request is rejected downstream. Wasted effort on both sides. *Detect:* Active items with no user criteria where entitlement differentiation exists elsewhere. *Confidence:* 100% on configuration. *Guard:* Genuinely universal catalogue. *Lane 2.*
Item descriptions that do not state what the requester receives

Requesters guess, order the wrong thing, and the rework appears as ITIL-010. *Detect:* Items with description length below threshold or matching the item name. *Confidence:* 90% — length and similarity checks. *Guard:* Self-evident items. *Lane 3.*
Pricing or cost absent where showback is in use

Consumption cannot be attributed to the consumer, which removes the demand signal that showback exists to create. *Detect:* Items with no cost attributes where a chargeback model exists. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Chargeback not applied to that category. *Lane 3.*

Two routes to the same thing with potentially different fulfilment and approval. Demand data splits. *Detect:* Items with matching normalised names or identical variable sets and fulfilment. *Confidence:* 85%. *Guard:* Deliberate variants by audience or entity. *Lane 3.* Joins DQ-116.
No catalogue governance or publication approval

Items are created and published with no review. The catalogue is the customer-facing surface of the entire service organisation, governed by nobody. *Detect:* Absence of an approval or review workflow on item publication. *Confidence:* 100% on configuration. *Guard:* Governance applied outside the platform. *Lane 2.*

Nobody knows whether the portal was up when requesters needed it. Catalogue downtime appears as suppressed demand rather than as an outage. *Detect:* Absence of availability measurement covering the portal or catalogue service. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Measured through external monitoring. *Lane 3.*
Knowledge base effectively unused — article-to-incident linkage near zero

Knowledge is written and never consumed. Every incident is resolved from first principles regardless of how many times it has occurred. *Detect:* Incidents with an article reference ÷ total incidents, against published article volume. *Confidence:* 100% on the ratio. *Guard:* Knowledge consumed through search without linkage being recorded — check whether linkage capture exists at all. *Lane 2.*
Knowledge suggestion not enabled on incident or request

Agents cannot see relevant articles at the point of need. Undermines the whole Known Error chain and makes ITIL-027 inevitable. *Detect:* Suggestion configuration disabled where published articles exist. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Surfaced through a different mechanism. *Lane 2.* Duplicates ITSM-015 deliberately — this is the practice-layer view.
Articles past review date still published

Guidance being followed that nobody has confirmed is still correct. Every incident resolved using it inherits the risk. *Detect:* Published articles with review date in the past, ranked by view volume. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Reviewed outside the platform without updating the field. *Lane 3.* Joins DQ-122.

Nobody is responsible for accuracy. The article ages indefinitely while remaining published. *Detect:* Published articles with empty owner or an inactive owner. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Ownership at knowledge base level. *Lane 3.*
Known Errors not published to knowledge

The Problem analysis exists and cannot be consumed. Agents resolving linked incidents cannot find the workaround written specifically for them. *Detect:* Known Error records with no published article. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Published in a separate system. *Lane 3.* Joins ITSM-066.
No knowledge creation from incident resolution

Resolutions are written into close notes and never promoted to knowledge. The organisation solves the same problem repeatedly and learns nothing structurally. *Detect:* Article creation rate against resolved incident volume and recurring cluster volume. *Confidence:* 100% on the rates. *Guard:* Knowledge authored through a separate editorial process. *Lane 3.*
Articles with zero views since publication

Either unfindable or irrelevant. Distinguish by comparing against the incident volume on the topic. *Detect:* Published articles with zero views beyond age threshold, against the incident volume matching their topic. *Confidence:* 100% on views; topic matching at 80%. *Guard:* Recently published. *Lane 3.*
Article feedback captured and never actioned

Users are telling you the article is wrong and nobody reads it. The feedback mechanism is a complaint channel with no recipient. *Detect:* Article feedback records with no subsequent article update. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Feedback actioned outside the record. *Lane 3.*
Duplicate articles covering the same topic

Search returns both, they diverge, and agents follow whichever ranks higher. *Detect:* Article pairs with content similarity above threshold. *Confidence:* 85%. *Guard:* Deliberate versions for different audiences. *Lane 3.*
No knowledge base for a service with high incident volume

The services generating the most repeated work have the least documented guidance. *Detect:* Services ranked by incident volume against article coverage for that service. *Confidence:* 90% — service-to-article mapping. *Guard:* Knowledge organised by technology rather than service. *Lane 3.*
Articles containing personal identifiers in free text

Knowledge articles are typically the most broadly readable content in the instance. Personal data there has the widest possible exposure. *Detect:* Article content matching identifier patterns with checksum validation where supported. *Confidence:* 95% validated, 75% pattern-only — report separately. *Evidence: count and location only, never the values.* *Guard:* Coincidental numeric strings. *Lane 3.* Joins DQ-133.
Knowledge workflow with no approval before publication

Anything published is authoritative to the person reading it. No review means incorrect guidance reaches agents and customers with no gate. *Detect:* Knowledge bases with publication workflow disabled or with no approval step. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Deliberate open-authoring model with post-publication review. *Lane 2.*
Retired articles still referenced from incident resolutions

Agents citing withdrawn guidance. *Detect:* Resolution article references to retired or unpublished articles. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Retired after the resolutions were written. *Lane 3.* Joins ITSM-139, DQ-131.

Article count is reported as a knowledge metric. Nobody measures whether knowledge reduces resolution time or deflects contact. *Detect:* Absence of deflection, resolution-time-with-article, or self-service success measurement. *Confidence:* 100% on measurement absence. *Guard:* Measured externally. *Lane 3.*

Service reports produced with no customer distribution

Compliance figures that omit uncovered priority bands, cancelled SLAs or unmeasured records overstate performance. No service level manager or accountable owner for SLM

Customer satisfaction not measured against service level performance

Technical compliance is reported without knowing whether the customer experienced good service. The two diverge more often than either party expects. *Detect:* Absence of satisfaction measurement correlated to service or SLA performance. *Confidence:* 100% on measurement absence. *Guard:* Measured externally. *Lane 3.*
Group 4 — Service Level Management as a Practice (ITIL-041 to 052)
Service level breaches with no root cause analysis

Breaches recur because nothing establishes why they happen. The SLM practice reports failure and does not reduce it. *Detect:* Breach clusters with no corresponding Problem record. *Confidence:* 100% on linkage. *Guard:* Cause established within the incident. *Lane 3.* Joins ITSM-054.

Service level targets inconsistent across comparable services

Two services of equivalent criticality carry materially different targets with no stated rationale. Release closed with no deployment verification

Group 5 — Release and Deployment Management (ITIL-053 to 066)

No definitive media library or artefact registry

Releases not traceable to demand, problem or change origin

Update sets promoted without release linkage

Group 5 — Release and Deployment Management (ITIL-053 to 066)
Release notes or deployment documentation absent

Failed releases with no post-implementation review

Recovery is attempted without a target, so nobody knows whether the outcome was acceptable. *Detect:* Critical services with no RTO or RPO recorded. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Defined in an external register. *Lane 3.*
RTO inconsistent with the supporting infrastructure's actual recovery capability

A four-hour RTO on infrastructure with a twelve-hour restore time. The objective is aspirational and nobody has reconciled it. *Detect:* Service RTO against the recovery characteristics of supporting CIs where recorded. *Confidence:* 90% — depends on infrastructure recovery data being captured. *Guard:* Compensating recovery path not modelled. *Lane 3.*

An untested plan is a document. The first execution is during the event, which is when discovery of its gaps is most expensive. *Detect:* Continuity plans with no test or exercise record within the test period. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Tested outside the platform with evidence. *Lane 3.*
Continuity plans not updated after significant change

The plan describes an architecture that no longer exists. Recovery follows steps that reference decommissioned components. *Detect:* Plans with no update since major changes to their supporting CI set. *Confidence:* 90%. *Guard:* Updated externally. *Lane 3.*
DR environment not represented in the CMDB

The recovery target is invisible to impact analysis, change control and capacity management. Changes to production do not propagate to DR because DR is not modelled. *Detect:* Services with continuity requirements and no DR-environment CIs. *Confidence:* 100% where environment tagging exists — gated by CMDB-016. *Guard:* DR managed by a provider outside the CMDB. *Lane 3.*

DR will not behave as production when invoked. This is exactly what cross-instance and cross-environment comparison detects, and nothing else does. *Detect:* Configuration comparison between production and DR CI sets for the same service. *Confidence:* 90% — requires DR environment data. *Guard:* Deliberate divergence with documented rationale. *Lane 3.*
Continuity dependencies on suppliers not documented

Recovery depends on a third party with no recorded obligation or contact path. *Detect:* Continuity plans for services with supplier dependencies and no linked supplier continuity terms. *Confidence:* 100% on linkage. *Guard:* Terms in contract records elsewhere. *Lane 3.*

The test identified gaps and the gaps remain. The organisation has documented evidence of known unremediated recovery risk, which is worse than not testing. *Detect:* Continuity test findings or actions open beyond age threshold. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Deferred with documented acceptance. *Lane 3.*
No continuity owner or invocation authority defined

At the moment of invocation, nobody has authority to declare. The delay while that is established is the most expensive delay in the whole recovery. *Detect:* Continuity plans with no owner or defined invocation authority. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Authority defined in an external policy. *Lane 3.*
Suppliers supporting critical services not registered

Third-party dependencies exist and are invisible. Supplier failure becomes a service outage with no prior assessment of the exposure. *Detect:* Services with external dependencies and no linked supplier record. *Confidence:* 90% — external dependency inference. *Guard:* Registered in a procurement system with linkage. *Lane 3.*
Contracts not linked to the services they support

Contract renewal, termination and performance are managed without knowing which services depend on them. *Detect:* Contract records with no service linkage, and services with supplier dependencies and no contract. *Confidence:* 100% on linkage. *Guard:* Mapping held externally. *Lane 3.*

Contractual terms exist and nothing evaluates them. Renewal negotiations proceed on impression rather than evidence. *Detect:* Contracts with performance terms and no measurement records. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Measured externally. *Lane 3.*
Contracts expiring within the notice period with no renewal action

Auto-renewal on unfavourable terms, or lapse of a service dependency. Both are avoidable and both are common. *Detect:* Contracts with expiry or notice dates approaching and no renewal task or decision record. *Confidence:* 100% on date arithmetic. *Guard:* Renewal managed in procurement. *Lane 3.*

Incidents caused by third parties are absorbed into internal metrics. The supplier's contribution to service failure is invisible at renewal. *Detect:* Incidents with vendor-related close codes and no supplier attribution. *Confidence:* 90% — close code classification. *Guard:* Attributed outside the record. *Lane 3.*
Supplier access to the platform not reviewed

Third-party users hold roles with no recertification. For a regulated entity this is an access control finding with regulatory weight. *Detect:* Users associated with supplier companies holding roles, against recertification records. *Confidence:* 100% on grants and review records. *Guard:* Reviewed in an external IGA platform. *Lane 3.* Joins PLT-134.
Supplier integrations with no documented owner or contract linkage

An integration to a third party with no recorded commercial relationship behind it. *Detect:* Outbound integrations to external endpoints with no supplier or contract linkage. *Confidence:* 90%. *Guard:* Linkage held externally. *Lane 3.* Joins PLT-153.
Underpinning contract terms not reconciled to service commitments

Covered structurally in ITIL-046; this is the practice-layer view — whether anyone performs the reconciliation as a recurring activity. *Detect:* Absence of a recurring reconciliation activity across contracts and service commitments. *Confidence:* 100% on activity absence. *Guard:* Performed externally. *Lane 3.*

Multiple critical services depending on one supplier. Knowable from the dependency graph and rarely computed. *Detect:* Supplier records ranked by the count and criticality of dependent services. *Confidence:* 100% where supplier-to-service linkage exists — gated by ITIL-106. *Guard:* Concentration accepted with documented mitigation. *Lane 3.*
Supplier exit or transition plans absent for critical dependencies

Termination or supplier failure has no planned response. The dependency is effectively permanent regardless of contract terms. *Detect:* Critical supplier dependencies with no exit or transition plan. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Plans held in procurement or GRC. *Lane 3.*
Contact channel volume not measured or differentiated

Phone, portal, email, chat and walk-up are not distinguished, so channel strategy has no data behind it. *Detect:* Contact type or channel field population across incidents and requests. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Single-channel operation. *Lane 2.*

Portal and knowledge investment is justified by deflection and deflection is not computed. *Detect:* Absence of deflection measurement against portal session and article view data. *Confidence:* 100% on measurement absence. *Guard:* Measured externally. *Lane 3.*
First contact resolution not measured or measured inconsistently

The primary service desk quality measure. Definitions vary widely and an inconsistent one is worse than none. *Detect:* Absence of FCR measurement, or definitional inconsistency across reports. *Confidence:* 100% on absence; 90% on inconsistency detection. *Guard:* Consistent definition held externally. *Lane 3.*
Abandonment or drop-off not measured on any channel

Contacts that never became tickets are invisible. Demand is understated by exactly the population that had the worst experience. *Detect:* Absence of abandonment measurement across telephony or portal session data. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Measured in the telephony platform. *Lane 3.*
Service desk operating with no defined scope or service hours

Expectations are set by experience rather than by agreement, and out-of-hours contacts have no defined handling. *Detect:* Absence of documented service hours or scope linked to the service desk service record. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Documented externally. *Lane 3.*
Escalation paths not defined or resolving to nobody

At the point of escalation there is no next step, or the next step is an empty group. *Detect:* Escalation configuration with no defined path, or paths resolving to inactive users or empty groups. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Escalation by convention. *Lane 3.*
Agent capacity not measured against demand
Staffing decisions are made without volume and handling time data. *Detect:* Absence of workload measurement against fulfiller capacity. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Measured in WFM. *Lane 3.*
Satisfaction survey response rate below the level that supports inference

Satisfaction is reported from a sample too small to mean anything, and the reported figure carries no confidence statement. *Detect:* Survey response rate against volume, with the resulting confidence interval. *Confidence:* 100% on the rate; state the interval alongside any satisfaction figure. *Guard:* Response rate adequate for the population. *Lane 3.*
No differentiation between service desk and technical queues in reporting

First-line and specialist performance are reported together, which flatters one and penalises the other. *Detect:* Reporting with no tier or queue-type differentiation. *Confidence:* 90%. *Guard:* Single-tier operation. *Lane 2.*
Major incident communication not routed through the service desk

During a major incident the service desk receives contacts about an event it has not been told about. Volume spikes and the desk has no information to give. *Detect:* Major incidents with no service desk communication task or notification. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Communication via an external channel. *Lane 2.* Joins ITSM-046.
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
No service portfolio distinct from the service catalogue

Pipeline and retired services are invisible. The organisation can see what it offers today and not what it is building or withdrawing. *Detect:* Absence of pipeline and retired lifecycle stages in the service record population. *Confidence:* 100% on the distribution. *Guard:* Portfolio managed in a PPM tool. *Lane 3.* Joins CSDM-017.
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)

Requests for new or changed services arrive as emails and conversations. Prioritisation has no visible backlog. *Detect:* Absence of demand records against change and project volume. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Demand in an external backlog. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
Demand not linked to the services it affects

The portfolio cannot show which services have pending change. Capacity and continuity planning have no forward view. *Detect:* Demand records with no service linkage. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Linkage in PPM. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
Service costs not attributed to services

Cost is tracked by cost centre and not by service, so no service has a total cost of ownership. Showback and value conversations have no basis. *Detect:* Services with no cost attribution, against the cost data available on their supporting CIs and assets. *Confidence:* 100% on attribution. *Guard:* Costing in a finance system. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
No chargeback or showback despite cost data being present

The data exists and the demand signal it would create is not produced. Consumers have no visibility of what they consume. *Detect:* Cost data present with no chargeback or showback configuration. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Showback external. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
Budget or funding not linked to services
Funding decisions are made without service-level cost and consumption data. *Detect:* Absence of budget linkage to service records. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Budgeting external. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)

The service is withdrawn and its infrastructure continues to bill. Straightforward, common, and directly monetisable as a finding. *Detect:* Retired-stage services with supporting CIs in an operational state carrying cost attributes. *Confidence:* 100% where cost data exists. *Guard:* Wind-down period. *Lane 3.* Joins CSDM-021.
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
Service investment not traceable to business outcome

Spend is recorded against services with no recorded objective or benefit. Value cannot be assessed at any level. *Detect:* Demand or investment records with no stated outcome or benefit measure. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Benefits tracked in PPM. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
Portfolio decisions made with no service performance data

Services are invested in or withdrawn without reference to their incident volume, availability or satisfaction. *Detect:* Portfolio lifecycle transitions with no correlated performance data reference. *Confidence:* 80% — absence of reference is circumstantial. *Guard:* Data considered outside the record. *Lane 3.*
Group 12 — Portfolio, Demand and Financial Management (ITIL-125 to 134)
No accountable owner for the service portfolio

Nobody owns the shape of the service estate, so it accretes rather than being designed. *Detect:* Absence of an assigned portfolio role. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Held within a broader role. *Lane 3.*

Improvement opportunities are identified in reviews and retrospectives and go nowhere. The practice exists as meetings with no artefact. *Detect:* Absence of an improvement record type or backlog with active entries. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Held in an external backlog. *Lane 3.*
Improvement items registered and never progressed

Worse than no register: a documented list of known problems the organisation chose not to fix, with the date each was identified. *Detect:* Improvement records with no state change beyond age threshold. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Deliberately deferred with documented acceptance. *Lane 3.*
Improvements not traceable to a measurement or finding

Improvement activity is driven by opinion rather than evidence. Effort goes where the loudest voice points. *Detect:* Improvement records with no linked metric, incident cluster, problem or assessment finding. *Confidence:* 100% on linkage. *Guard:* Evidence in the discussion record. *Lane 3.*
Improvements closed with no measured outcome

The change was made and nobody confirmed it improved anything. Identical in shape to ITSM-074, applied to the improvement practice itself. *Detect:* Closed improvements with no before-and-after measurement recorded. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Measured externally. *Lane 3.*
Post-incident review actions not feeding the improvement register

The most evidence-rich source of improvement is disconnected from the improvement practice. *Detect:* PIR actions with no corresponding improvement record. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Managed within the PIR. *Lane 3.* Joins ITSM-052.
No baseline captured before an improvement initiative

Without a before, there is no after. Improvement outcomes become assertions. *Detect:* Improvement records with no baseline measurement recorded at initiation. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Baseline held externally. *Lane 3.*
Improvement activity concentrated in one area while defects concentrate elsewhere

Effort and need are misaligned. Detectable by comparing the improvement backlog against the finding distribution. *Detect:* Improvement record distribution against the assessment finding distribution by domain. *Confidence:* 100% on both distributions; the misalignment conclusion is advisory. *Guard:* Deliberate sequencing. *Lane 3.*
No accountable owner for continual improvement
The practice is everyone's responsibility and therefore nobody's. *Detect:* Absence of an assigned improvement role. *Confidence:* 100%. *Guard:* Held within a broader role. *Lane 3.*
Practices operating with no shared service model

Incident, request, change, release, continuity and supplier management each reference services differently or not at all. There is no single view of a service across the practices that support it. *Detect:* Service reference consistency across all practice record types. *Confidence:* 100% on the reference rates. *Guard:* Deliberate decoupling. *Lane 2 across practices.* Joins ITSM-129.
Request fulfilment creating CIs outside the configuration practice

Provisioning through the catalogue creates infrastructure with no CMDB registration, no owner and no lifecycle. The catalogue becomes a shadow provisioning path. *Detect:* Fulfilment workflows creating or provisioning resources with no CMDB registration step. *Confidence:* 95%. *Guard:* Registration by subsequent discovery — verify discovery covers the target. *Lane 2.* Joins ITOM-134.
Knowledge, Problem and Incident not forming a closed loop

Incidents recur, Problems are not raised, Known Errors are not written, knowledge is not consumed. Each link in the learning chain is broken independently and the aggregate effect is that the organisation does not learn. *Detect:* The four ratios end to end — incident recurrence, problem creation, known error publication, article consumption — reported together. *Confidence:* 100% on each ratio. *Guard:* Loop closed through an external mechanism. *Lane 3.*
Availability and continuity commitments not reconciled to infrastructure reality

The service promises an availability target and an RTO, and the dependency graph shows a single point of failure with a longer recovery time. Both commitments are undeliverable and the evidence to prove it already exists. *Detect:* Service availability targets and RTOs against dependency-graph redundancy and recorded recovery characteristics. *Confidence:* 90% — gated by relationship completeness. *Guard:* Compensating arrangements not modelled. *Lane 3.*
Practice maturity inconsistent across the service lifecycle

Strong incident management with absent problem, release and continuity practice. The organisation is good at responding and poor at preventing, and the imbalance is measurable rather than anecdotal. *Detect:* Practice-level scores across all groups, reported as a profile rather than a single number. *Confidence:* Composite of underlying confidences. *Guard:* Deliberate maturity prioritisation. *No lane — composite metric.*
Practices measured but not governed — metrics with no owner and no action threshold

The estate produces extensive reporting and nothing triggers action. This is the finding that most often explains why an organisation has good dashboards and poor outcomes, and it is the natural closing statement of an ITIL assessment. *Detect:* Reported metrics against defined owners, thresholds and correlated action records. *Confidence:* 100% on ownership and threshold configuration; 80% on action correlation. *Guard:* Governance conducted outside the platform with evidence. *Lane 3.*
